newsitem.title: UK: Airlines buy fuel in biggest spree since Gulf War.
newsitem.headline: Airlines buy fuel in biggest spree since Gulf War.

text.p: World airlines have snapped up more than a million tonnes of jet fuel in a buying spree over the past couple of weeks that dwarfs anything seen since the Gulf War sent prices rocketing six years ago, said oil traders in London.

Soaring demand for jet fuel and a 15 percent slump in the price of crude oil over the past month have triggered an intense bout of competitive buying among airlines eager to take advantage of an economic upturn in the West.

"The last time I saw this kind of buying was around Christmas just before the fighting began in the Gulf War," said Nigel Saperia, managing director of Bankers Trust International in London who said the total volume bought was well over a million tonnes.
Typically, the market might take two months to rack up those kinds of sales, said dealers. Airlines have been buying swaps which enable them to lock in forward fuel costs for fuel used next summer.

Worldwide demand for jet fuel and kerosene rose nearly six percent in 1996 from 1995 levels, the International Energy Agency (IEA), the West's oil watchdog, last week. This compares with an average rise for all oil products of just two percent.

"Over the last couple of weeks we've seen a million tonnes hedged on a wide range of paper contracts," said Paul Ford, head of financing products at the Royal Bank of Scotland, a leading swaps provider to the airlines.
"In a typical week we would hope to write four or five jet deals but recently we have been doing that number every day" he said.

Although falling oil prices have encouraged the latest round of buying, jet fuel prices have recently been well above year ago levels. Privately, many oil companies are delighted at the latest demand, given the fragile interest in other high value oil products like gasoline and heating oil.
"I can't understand why they (the airlines) are buying now. They have been paying well above last year's levels," said one trader.

In Europe jet fuel prices averaged about $210 a tonne during the second and third quarters last year. The same period this year is currently talking about $206 but most deals have been locked in between $210 and $220 over the past two weeks, said traders.
The reason for the recent buying spree may have origins in a meeting of the world airline body last November.
Then, International Air Transport Association (IATA) called an emergency meeting of its 250 member airlines on November 13 to consider "concerted action" to counter rising fuel costs.
"It is an emergency situation. Fuel costs have been going up pretty steadily this year," IATA spokesman Tim Goodyear said in November.

The average worldwide price of fuel paid by IATA members during the first nine months of 1996 was 73.9 cents per U.S. gallon, against 65.2 cents in 1995, he added. Internationally scheduled services spend $13 billion a year on aviation fuel.
"If the fuel price goes up 10 percent, that is an extra $1.3 billion compared with airlines profits last year of $5.2 billion," Goodyear said.

Fears of rising jet fuel prices may also lies close to the surface after last year's unexpected spike in prices. Spot prices averaged $160 a tonne in 1995 but soared to an average of nearer $220 last year.
During the summer, prices rocketed by nearly $100 a tonne to peak at nearly $280 in the space of just over three months.
